issues.legal_issue: A worshipper may maintain a suit for a declaration that a compromise decree is not binding on a temple even if the worshipper does not claim a legal character or property right within the declaratory-relief statute.
material_facts: The plaintiff brought the suit as a worshipper of the temple and sought a declaration that a compromise decree concerning temple properties was not binding on the deity.
The declaration, if granted, would restore the deity’s rights in the trust properties.
issues.conclusion: The suit was maintainable because the requested declaration was substantial relief with immediate coercive effect and fell outside the scope of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877.
issues.legal_principle: Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877 is not exhaustive of the cases in which declaratory decrees may be granted; courts may grant declarations independently of its requirements under the general provisions of the Civil Procedure Code. The Court relied on Fischer v. Secretary of State for India in Council and Pratap Singh v. Bhabuti Singh; distinguished Sheoparsan Singh v. Ramnandan Prasad Singh; and applied the principle that worshippers, as spiritual beneficiaries, may seek a declaration that an improper alienation is not binding on a deity, as reflected in Vidhyapurna Thirthaswami v. Vidhyanidhi Thirthaswami, Kalyana Venkataramana Ayyangar v. Kasturiranga Ayyangar, Chidambaranatha Thambiran v. Nallasiva Mudaliar, and Abdur Rahim v. Mahomed Barkat Ali.

predicates.suit_by_temple_worshipper: A worshipper of a temple brought the suit to protect the interests of its deity.
predicates.suit_seeks_declaration_decree_not_bindin: The suit seeks a declaration that a decree concerning temple interests does not bind the deity.
predicates.declaration_restores_deity_trust_rights: The requested declaration would restore or protect the deity’s rights in trust property.

issues.definition: When a worshipper seeks a declaration that a decree does not bind the deity and that declaration would restore or protect the deity’s trust rights, the suit is maintainable.

issues.legal_issue: A compromise decree concerning temple interests does not bind the deity when the deity was not represented in the proceeding by a person legally authorized to represent it.
material_facts: The Commissioner of Endowments was a party to the proceeding in which the compromise decree was recorded.
The deity was not made a party through a representative, and the court did not appoint a disinterested next friend to represent it.
The Commissioner’s statutory powers were powers of superintendence and control over the temple.
issues.conclusion: The compromise decree was not binding on the deity because the Commissioner had no authority, on the basis of those powers, to represent it in the proceeding, and the deity had no other representative there.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 20 of the Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1927, the Commissioner’s superintendence and control over the temple did not confer authority to represent the deity in proceedings under section 84(2). Ordinarily, the deity is represented by its shebait; where the shebait is negligent or adverse to the deity’s interests, a worshipper or other interested person may bring proceedings for the deity as next friend, and a disinterested next friend may be appointed by the court. The Court relied on Pramath Nath v. Pradymna Kumar.

predicates.statutory_temple_status_proceeding: The proceeding concerns the legal status or administration of a temple under a statutory process.
predicates.deity_interests_affected_by_compromise: A compromise in the proceeding determines or affects rights claimed for the deity.
predicates.deity_not_represented_by_authorized_pers: The deity was not represented by its shebait or, where appropriate, by a next friend acting for its interests.

issues.definition: When a compromise in a statutory temple-status proceeding affects the deity’s interests and the deity was not represented by an authorized person, the compromise does not bind the deity.

issues.legal_issue: A compromise decree cannot grant a declaration of personal ownership of property when that relief is outside the scope of the statutory proceeding in which the compromise is made.
material_facts: The original proceeding sought to set aside an administrative order classifying the temple as public and to obtain a declaration that it was private.
The petition was amended to seek a further declaration that the disputed properties were the petitioners’ personal property rather than temple property.
The compromise decree included that personal-ownership declaration.
issues.conclusion: The personal-ownership declaration was outside the scope of the proceeding under section 84(2) of the Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1927, and the compromise decree was therefore not valid or binding on the temple.
issues.legal_principle: Section 84(2) of the Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1927 provided a proceeding to challenge the Board’s order concerning the temple’s status; it did not authorize a declaration that disputed properties were the petitioners’ personal property. A decree granting relief beyond the scope of the proceeding cannot bind the temple as to that relief.

predicates.statutory_challenge_to_temple_status: The proceeding is a statutory challenge to an administrative determination of a temple’s status.
predicates.compromise_grants_property_ownership_rel: The compromise grants a declaration determining that disputed property belongs personally to a party rather than to the temple.
predicates.property_ownership_relief_outside_procee: The statutory proceeding does not authorize the court to determine that personal-ownership claim.

issues.definition: When a compromise in a statutory challenge to temple status grants property-ownership relief that the proceeding does not authorize, the compromise is not valid or binding on the temple.
